leading_positions.synthesis: Four members explicitly prefer Anne Carson as sole laureate. They share the grounds of a recognisable voice, formal invention that carries emotional and intellectual weight, and a practice in which philology, translation, essay and verse form one method. They most often cite Autobiography of Red and Nox. They do not share one citation scope. Carlberg's wording names lyric, verse narrative, essay, translation and elegy. Olsson's names a poetic, essayistic and translational oeuvre. Palm's adds 'the book itself'. Sward's anchors the claim in original poetry and essays and treats translation as part of the same practice. All four state reservations: dependence on typography and book-object form, a fragmentary corpus, possible mannerism in later work, and whether the hybrid mode fits the 'ideal direction' of Nobel's will. Each of these reservations is stated as unresolved.

Two members explicitly prefer Mircea Cărtărescu as sole laureate. They share the grounds of a distinctive voice, a coherent metaphysical project built from memory, the body and dream, and ambition across poetry and the large novels (Blinding, Solenoid). Their citations differ in scope. Mattson's names prose and poetry together as an imaginative architecture. Sem-Sandberg's traces a line from the poetry through the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. Both concede that they judge Romanian sentence-level density only through translation and secondary reading, and that repetition or unevenness in the long late novels is not ruled out. They differ slightly on evidence: Mattson says the late novels do not simply repeat the earlier books, while Sem-Sandberg says he cannot confirm this from direct reading. Both name Carson as an alternative.

areas_of_agreement: All six files name both Carson (B004) and Cărtărescu (B028) as either the preferred candidate or a first or second alternative, so the round 1 discussion concentrates on a two-candidate comparison. Round 1 files do not contest the literary seriousness of either writer.

Every member's configuration names exactly one laureate on a single prize part, and each ballot ID carries one credited name. No member proposes a multiwriter configuration or a different laureate under B004 or B028.

All members state that their judgments of Carson's design-dependent books, Cărtărescu's Romanian prose and other non-English corpora rest on public knowledge and translation. None claims to have independently verified a source.
Several members state that volume or bulk is not a merit criterion in itself, and that the relevant test is whether quality and development are sustained across the oeuvre.

Members on both sides treat the 'ideal direction' of Nobel's will as a question to be argued on literary grounds, and they apply it as a test of depth and seriousness of imaginative purpose rather than of subject matter. Several explicitly decline to read it as excluding learned or experimental work.
No member reports a personal, professional or family tie to a shortlisted writer that would call for recusal.
scientific_disputes: Carson: whether the hybrid, scholarly and book-object mode amounts to sustained imaginative depth or is sometimes erudite or mannered play. Sem-Sandberg and Mattson press this most directly, and Carson's supporters concede the risk without regarding it as refuting her case.

Carson: how much of her effect survives translation and standard editions, given dependence on typography, layout and the relation to Greek and Latin texts. Mattson also observes that the achievement should not reduce to the book as a material object.

Cărtărescu: whether the long digressive structures show an accumulating, controlled design or a lack of economy and a drift toward repetition. Olsson and Carlberg raise the concern, and Mattson and Sem-Sandberg answer it as a matter of method.

Standard of comparison: whether concentrated, formally exact and continually renewed work (Carson, Michon) or large-scale imaginative construction in a single voice (Cărtărescu) better meets the whole-oeuvre standard. Members describe this as a disagreement about weighting more than about talent.

Michon appears only as an alternative for Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Palm, who note limits of translation and of a compact corpus. Adonis is named as an alternative by Carlberg and Olsson, and Tawada as an alternative by Sward. The round 1 files give little developed argument for any of these cases on literary grounds.
attribution_disputes: Carson: whether translations, adaptations and versions of Greek texts belong to the core literary achievement or sit at its margin. Carlberg and Olsson treat translation and original verse as one practice, and Olsson would credit the whole practice without claiming the translations as independent creation. Sward would anchor the citation in original poetry and essays. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg treat the question as unresolved and as affecting how broad Carson's claim is.

Proposed citations for B004 differ in whether they name translation (Carlberg and Olsson do; Sward subordinates it; Palm's does not mention it), whether they name the book as a form (Palm), and whether they name drama or later work. Carlberg would limit the claim to the established core and would not claim that recent work equals it.

Citation drafting for B028 differs in whether it leads with poetry (Sem-Sandberg) or names prose and poetry together (Mattson). Sem-Sandberg also suggests that a Carson citation, if one is drafted, should name poetry first.
No member disputes author identity or proposes additional names or organisations. The differences concern citation scope for the same writer.
maturity_disputes: Carson: whether work after roughly 2010 keeps the level of the 1990s and 2000s books. Olsson raises this, referring to a peak in roughly 1998-2010. Carlberg, Palm and Sward say it is unverified and would test it. Sem-Sandberg says it strengthens his reservation that her case rests on a stable core of acknowledged texts.

Cărtărescu: whether the late large novels develop or repeat earlier motifs. Mattson says they do not repeat and that the project is still developing. Sem-Sandberg cannot confirm this and wants specific volumes tested. Both acknowledge thinner coverage of the poetry and early work.

Whether a smaller or more fragmentary corpus, such as Carson's or Michon's, meets the 'sustained quality' and 'significance across the body of work' standard, and whether the case then falls on a handful of books (Autobiography of Red, Nox).
Carlberg's file notes that the tension between concentrated work and bulk is unresolved and also bears on the Cărtărescu and Michon comparisons.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: No member's file identifies a conflict requiring recusal.

Carlberg is a co-opted member whose actual committee voting status is undocumented. Her simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and her explicit position (B004) counts in the tally above only on that assumption.

Chair disclosure: the chair's own round 1 position is B004 with alternatives B028 and B044. This summary is a process summary and not a ruling. His stated scholarly interests in the fragment, translation and exile literature overlap thematically with parts of Carson's practice. His file treats this as context and not as a conflict or evidence of preference.

Several members mention their own literary practice (Carlberg on archival non-fiction, Mattson on historical and dream-logic fiction, Sem-Sandberg on writing about Central Europe) as context only. None presents it as a connection to a shortlisted writer. Sward notes that her shared first name with Carson is coincidental.
questions_for_round2: For B004: which specific Carson works form the core on which the citation rests, and does the citation name translation, and if so how? Should it be limited to original poetry, verse narrative, elegy and essay, as Carlberg and Sward propose, or to the whole practice, as Olsson proposes? Can the members who have read the later books (after about 2010) say whether they keep the level of the core?

For B028: which specific Cărtărescu volumes, among the late novels and the poetry or early work, can members test directly to decide whether the maximalism develops or repeats? Can Mattson and Sem-Sandberg, who prefer him, say what evidence beyond translation and reception would settle the question of economy and control?

Before comparing Carson and Cărtărescu again, can each member state the standard they apply to 'sustained quality across the oeuvre' and to the 'ideal direction' in Nobel's will, and then apply the same test to both candidates? Does that standard favour concentrated formal renewal or large-scale imaginative construction, and what would change a member's ranking?

How should the committee compare a writer judged in English (Carson) with writers whose strongest qualities, by members' own account, lie in Romanian syntax (Cărtărescu), Arabic prosody (Adonis) or French sentence texture (Michon), when reading competence is uneven? Is any further reading in the original or in additional translations available or needed before round 2 positions are fixed?

Adonis (B044) is named as an alternative by Carlberg and Olsson, and Michon (B015) by Mattson, Palm and Sem-Sandberg. Can their supporters argue the literary case for each, covering voice, formal achievement, sustained quality and whole-oeuvre significance, so that these cases can be weighed against the two leading positions?

Do any members who currently prefer one of the two leading candidates, or who named one as a first alternative, see a citation scope or reading of the evidence under which they would change their order? If so, which specific point would they need to see resolved?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows two explicit leading positions: four members (Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Sward) prefer Carson, and two (Mattson, Sem-Sandberg) prefer Cărtărescu. The files do not record any other explicit first preference, and nothing here infers hidden votes. Every member names both writers among their preferred candidate and alternatives, and the reservations stated about each are mostly the same ones: translation dependence, corpus shape, sustained quality and the reading of Nobel's will. These are round 1 statements and not final votes, and the simulated committee recommendation does not replace the decision of the full Swedish Academy. The chair's own position is disclosed above. Round 2 would be most useful if it concentrated on testable points (the later Carson books, specific Cărtărescu volumes, the exact citation scope) and on a common standard applied to every shortlisted writer, including those with little developed argument so far.
